content:
# Car still burning oil after replacing head gasket and rings; what's next?

You've swapped the head gasket set and piston rings on your 1991 BMW E34 525i, yet the engine is still consuming oil. The absence of external leaks suggests the internal consumption is real, but the lack of visible smoke under load indicates the severity might be lower than a catastrophic failure or that the issue lies elsewhere in the breathing system. On an engine with 374,000 km, replacing rings and gaskets is standard procedure for high-mileage maintenance, but it is not a guaranteed cure-all if other sealing surfaces remain compromised.

The piston ring replacement alone does not account for the entire oil control system. While the compression rings seal the combustion chamber and scrape excess oil from the cylinder walls, the oil control rings often require specific attention during reassembly. If you did not install new oil control ring expander clips or if the tensioners were not properly seated, the rings may not expand fully to contact the cylinder wall. This is a common oversight that leads to immediate post-repair oil burning. Ensure the third groove in the piston has a fresh set of oil rings and that the tensioner springs are functional.

Another frequent culprit in engines of this age is the valve stem seals. Even if you replaced the head gasket, you may have left the original valve stem seals untouched, or they may have degraded during the removal process. When these seals fail, oil drips down the valve guides into the combustion chamber and burns off immediately upon ignition. This often manifests as blue smoke on startup after a cold sit, rather than heavy smoke under acceleration. Since you reported little smoke while accelerating, this suggests the rings are doing their job relatively well, but the static consumption from the valve stems could still be significant over time.

The Positive Crankcase Ventilation (PCV) system is another critical path to investigate. On the M20 engine found in your E34 525i, a clogged or failing PCV valve creates excessive crankcase pressure. This pressure forces oil vapor past the piston rings and out through the breather system, mimicking ring failure. If the oil filler cap is difficult to remove due to high pressure, or if you see sludge buildup around the valve cover gasket, the PCV system is likely restricted. Replacing the PCV valve and ensuring the breathers are clear can sometimes resolve burning oil issues without further disassembly.

Finally, consider the cylinder wall condition. If the cylinders were not honed to a proper surface finish or if they are out of round due to heat cycles over 374,000 km, new rings will not seal effectively. Rings need a specific cross-hatch pattern on the cylinder walls to maintain tension and oil control. If you installed rings without verifying the cylinder bore dimensions (SAE #1, #2, or standard), you might have simply swapped bad parts for slightly different bad parts. Measuring the cylinders with a bore gauge is essential before concluding the job is done.

If the valve stems, PCV system, and ring installation are all confirmed correct, and the burning persists at an unacceptable rate, you must accept that the cylinder walls may be scored or tapered beyond repair. At this point, boring out the cylinders to oversize the bores and installing new pistons becomes the only viable option for restoring long-term reliability.

While mechanical repairs on older air-cooled or early water-cooled BMWs are labor-intensive, addressing the root cause of oil consumption is vital for protecting your investment.
